- U9 (hybrid: one-kernel-iteration ROI): **DONE** 2026-07-16 - the
  roadmap's primary goal, met: real `llama-completion` runs under
  `./andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --runtime linux`, cycle-
  accurate leg measures one real matmul, **6528953 cycles**, reproducible
  across 2 independent runs. Small matvec fixture (`rt_linux_matvec.c`,
  13739 cycles, wired into the automated sweep) verified the core
  mechanism first, same two-step pattern as every other U-feature.

  **Mechanism gap fixed (driver-only, zero vsim source changes, per the
  roadmap's own constraint)**: vsim's `CsrTrigger` statically pre-scans
  its OWN boot ELF for markers at configure time (LIEF), so it never sees
  markers inside a dynamically-loaded `--runtime linux` app. Fixed with
  `driver/elf_syms.{hpp,cpp}`'s new `find_roi_markers()` (reuses the
  SAME shared `include/hybrid/insn_match.h` both QEMU's plugin and vsim
  already use - no reimplementation drift) + `cmd_run.cpp` converting
  vsim's leg from marker- to the EXISTING `--hybrid-exit-pc` PC-trigger
  flag when `--runtime linux` is active. QEMU's leg stays marker-based
  (its plugin watches the executed stream, no such gap).

  **New CLI flag, `--step-timeout-ms`**: `PlanOptions.timeout_ms` was a
  hardcoded 90000 with no override - fine for fixtures, not for a real
  transformer matmul on the ~8.6kHz cycle leg (needs minutes). Added
  table-driven like `--mem-size`, RED test first in `cli_test.cpp`
  (compile failure), threaded into `PlanOptions` in `cmd_run.cpp`, new
  black-box test `test_andes_sim_step_timeout.sh`.

  **Getting the REAL llama-completion binary through it: four genuine
  illegal-instruction (mcause=2) sites**, same "fast-permissive/cycle-
  enforces" bug family as U3/U4/U5 but at the ELEN/vector-unit level -
  hybrid's QEMU leg is engine-synced (`elen=32`), unlike fast mode's own
  unconstrained cpu string, so QEMU1 itself now enforces the real vector
  width limit fast mode never did:
  1. `ggml_vec_dot_f16`/`ggml_vec_dot_bf16` (llama.cpp `vec.cpp`): GCC
     auto-vectorizes their scalar `double`-accumulated fallback loop into
     illegal e64. Fixed with `__attribute__((target("arch=rv64gc")))` on
     just those two functions - confirmed empirically this works on this
     GCC/RISC-V (14.3.0) when `optimize` attribute and `#pragma GCC
     push_options` do NOT (both tried, objdump-verified no change either
     way).
  2. `ggml_vec_cvar_f32`/`ggml_vec_soft_max_f32` (same file): explicit
     `vfloat64m1_t` widening-reduce accumulator, unlike every OTHER
     architecture's branch in the SAME two functions (which reduce in f32
     then widen ONE scalar per chunk in plain C) - a real inconsistency
     with its own siblings, not a hardware need. Fixed by matching the
     sibling pattern (non-widening f32 reduce + scalar widen).
  3. `quantize_row_q8_0`/`quantize_row_q8_1` (llama.cpp `arch/riscv/
     quants.c`): hardcoded LMUL=8 for a FLOAT op (`vfabs`/`vfredmax`);
     `ax45mpv_premium`'s vector FPU datapath doesn't reach LMUL=8 for
     float (confirmed: an INTEGER load at the same LMUL=8 executes fine
     right before the float op faults - FP-datapath-specific, correlates
     with the engine's `isa-vl4` config bit). Per TDD.md's "remove and
     rewrite": both now call their existing portable `_ref` scalar
     implementations unconditionally, not a build-flag suppression (no
     compiler flag could pick a smaller-LMUL alternative that doesn't
     exist in this code). Only ~1/650th of the matmul's actual work
     (activation quantization once per row, reused by the dot-product
     loop), so this cost nothing measurable.
  4. Stale ccache / incomplete incremental rebuild (not a code bug, a
     process trap): `compile_commands.json` showing the right `-march`
     was NOT sufficient evidence the `.o` had actually been recompiled -
     `find -delete` + rebuild silently did not reproduce one object file;
     only an explicit `rm -f` of its exact path forced real recompilation.
     Cost real debugging time before being recognized as a build-cache
     artifact, not a fix that "didn't work."

  **Diagnosability gap found and fixed while root-causing #3** (which
  only manifests on vsim, not QEMU1, so needed vsim's own stderr):
  `runtime/handler.c`'s shared trap handler calls `fprintf` then
  `_exit()` - `_exit()` never flushes stdio, so on vlinux's fully-
  buffered stderr the WHOLE diagnostic was silently lost on every trap,
  not just this session's. Fixed with `fflush(stderr)` before `_exit()`
  (a real permanent fix) plus a new `raw_print_hex()` using the existing
  `htif_uart_putc()` directly (no stdio/malloc) to print mcause/mepc/mtval
  BEFORE even attempting fprintf - cheap insurance for a future trap
  whose corrupted state might take fprintf itself out. Separately
  observed (not fixed, orthogonal): the `andesim` driver's own capture of
  a spawned subprocess's stdout silently dropped vsim's raw output in at
  least one path during this investigation; invoking `sim_ax45mpv_premium`
  directly (bypassing the driver) is what surfaced it. Worth a future
  driver-side look if it recurs.

  **ROI target selection - the roadmap's own "confirm actual figure once
  measured" note, taken literally**: the original K=50 pick (layer 7's Q
  projection, 2560->4096) is real, correct, e64-free code once the above
  4 fixes land, but too large for the cycle-accurate leg to finish even
  inside 900000ms (15 min). Rather than keep raising the timeout blindly,
  dumped every mul_mat's operand shapes for one real forward pass on a
  NATIVE x86 build (fast, no simulator - a throwaway env-gated fprintf,
  reverted after use) and ranked relative cost: FFN gate/up/down (2560x9728)
  are actually ~2.4x LARGER than Q, not smaller; K/V-projection (2560x1024,
  this model's grouped-query attention) is the smallest matmul shape
  anywhere in the architecture, ~4x fewer MACs than Q. Retargeted to K=51
  (the very next node, layer 7's V projection) via a plain `-D` reconfigure
  (no source change) - completed comfortably inside budget both times.

  Full details (exact code diffs, the size-dump technique, the marker
  patch snippet) in `docs/llama_roi_howto.md` (new) and the roadmap's own
  U9 DONE note (longer, blow-by-blow). `docs/USER_GUIDE.md` section 11
  updated with the confirmed command + cycle figure; a new section 5.11
  documents `--step-timeout-ms` (existing 5.11/5.12 renumbered to
  5.12/5.13, cross-references updated).
- U10, U11: PLANNED, explicitly optional/parallel, only needed if Bonsai-27B
  is revisited later.

3	description: QEMU's functional/MMIO model silently tolerates real-hardware-contract violations (missing fence.i, stale gp, misaligned device access) that vsim's cycle-accurate RTL correctly faults on -- always verify new low-level code on the cycle leg, not just fast.
4	metadata:
5	  type: feedback
6	  originSessionId: 5eeca9dc-9078-4a2c-9aec-f331d1142619
7	---
8	
9	Recurring bug class in the vlinux/hybrid work (3 occurrences across
10	[[andesim-linux-runtime-roadmap]] U3, U4, U5, same root shape each time):
11	code that violates a real RISC-V/hardware contract passes cleanly on the
12	**fast** leg (QEMU) because QEMU's functional model is permissive, then
13	fails -- often confusingly, via a trap or a hang, not an obvious "wrong
14	value" -- on the **cycle** leg (vsim, real RTL) because that engine
15	actually enforces the contract.
16	
17	Concrete instances:
18	1. **Missing `fence.i`** after writing freshly-loaded code via ordinary
19	   guest stores (U3): QEMU has no I-cache model, so stale/empty fetch
20	   never happens there; vsim's real cache faulted with an illegal
21	   instruction. Required by the RISC-V spec whenever a hart writes then
22	   executes new code.
23	2. **Stale `gp` in a trap handler** (U4): `trap.S` never reloaded `gp` to
24	   the handler's own `__global_pointer$` before running C trap-handler
25	   code, so gp-relative global access used whatever gp was active at trap
26	   time (the app's gp, once the app is running) instead of the handler's
27	   own. Silent on both engines UNTIL the trap handler's C code actually
28	   touched a global variable -- functionally this is engine-independent,
29	   but it was found in a cycle-leg debugging session precisely because
30	   fast/cycle divergence is the standing way these bugs get caught.
31	3. **Misaligned/sub-width HTIF window access** (U5): `htif_win_load` is
32	   documented (`runtime/htif_client.h`) as u64-load-only with an
33	   8-aligned `woff` requirement (it dereferences a `uint64_t*` at
34	   `WIN_DATA_VA+woff`). A 4-byte read at a non-8-aligned offset returned
35	   the right bytes on QEMU's byte-addressable MMIO model, then faulted
36	   (mcause=5, load access fault, mtval pointing exactly at the bad
37	   address) on vsim's real uncached-device bus logic.
38	
39	**Why**: QEMU is a functional simulator (correct architectural state,
40	permissive about HOW you got there); vsim is cycle-accurate RTL (models
41	the real bus/cache/pipeline, so it enforces every real hardware
42	constraint: natural alignment on device accesses, I-cache coherency
43	needing explicit fences, whatever register state actually happens to be
44	live at a given PC). QEMU passing is necessary but never sufficient
45	evidence that low-level RISC-V/device code is correct.
46	
47	**How to apply**: for any new code that (a) writes then executes memory,
48	(b) touches global/static state from a trap/handler context, or (c) does
49	raw MMIO/window/register-window access at a sub-natural width or a
50	computed (non-obviously-aligned) offset -- do not trust a fast-leg-only
51	pass. Run the cycle leg before calling such a feature done. When a
52	cycle-leg failure looks bizarre (silent hang, fault at an odd address,
53	wrong value read back) and the SAME code passed on fast, suspect this
54	class first: check for a missing fence.i, a stale register assumed live
55	across a context switch, or a violated access-width/alignment contract,
56	before assuming a logic bug in the new code itself.

Recurring bug class in the vlinux/hybrid work (3 occurrences across
[[andesim-linux-runtime-roadmap]] U3, U4, U5, same root shape each time):
code that violates a real RISC-V/hardware contract passes cleanly on the
**fast** leg (QEMU) because QEMU's functional model is permissive, then
fails -- often confusingly, via a trap or a hang, not an obvious "wrong
value" -- on the **cycle** leg (vsim, real RTL) because that engine
actually enforces the contract.

Concrete instances:
1. **Missing `fence.i`** after writing freshly-loaded code via ordinary
   guest stores (U3): QEMU has no I-cache model, so stale/empty fetch
   never happens there; vsim's real cache faulted with an illegal
   instruction. Required by the RISC-V spec whenever a hart writes then
   executes new code.
2. **Stale `gp` in a trap handler** (U4): `trap.S` never reloaded `gp` to
   the handler's own `__global_pointer$` before running C trap-handler
   code, so gp-relative global access used whatever gp was active at trap
   time (the app's gp, once the app is running) instead of the handler's
   own. Silent on both engines UNTIL the trap handler's C code actually
   touched a global variable -- functionally this is engine-independent,
   but it was found in a cycle-leg debugging session precisely because
   fast/cycle divergence is the standing way these bugs get caught.
3. **Misaligned/sub-width HTIF window access** (U5): `htif_win_load` is
   documented (`runtime/htif_client.h`) as u64-load-only with an
   8-aligned `woff` requirement (it dereferences a `uint64_t*` at

   the right bytes on QEMU's byte-addressable MMIO model, then faulted

   fast mode's own hardcoded `-cpu andes-ax45mpv,vlen=512` (no `elen`

   accumulated scalar fallback loops (`ggml_vec_dot_f16`/`_bf16` in

   under fast's unconstrained cpu string, illegal-instruction (mcause=2)

   branch in the same functions reduces in native precision and widens
   only the final scalar) -- same symptom, different root (an upstream
   algorithmic inconsistency, not a compiler auto-vectorization artifact).

---
name: pipe-swallows-build-exit-code
description: "Piping a build to tail/head swallows its exit code; use pipefail or no pipe, and verify the log for errors before trusting \"exit 0\""
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 2035c5f1-f922-474b-aaa8-0263551b122f
---

`bash build_vsim.sh 2>&1 | tail -5` returns tail's exit code (0), not the
build's. Two vsim rebuilds in one session reported "completed exit 0" while
ninja had actually stopped on a compile error -- the stale binaries then sent
debugging in circles for ~30 minutes.

**Why:** a pipeline's exit code is the LAST command's. `tail` always exits 0,
so any `build | tail` looks successful.

**How to apply:**
- When piping a build (especially `run_in_background` where only the exit code
  comes back), prefix `set -o pipefail`, or don't pipe at all and read the
  output file afterward.
- On any "successful" build, if downstream behavior looks stale (old binary
  semantics, missing symbols/strings), grep the build log for
  `error|build stopped` BEFORE debugging the code. Check `.ninja_log` /
  object-file mtimes to confirm the target actually recompiled.
- This applies to the vsim container build (`build_vsim.sh`, [[andes-engine-config-source]]
  relates: engines are rebuilt per config) and any long build piped for brevity.

**Related, distinct gotcha (2026-07-16, llama.cpp riscv build,
[[andesim-linux-runtime-roadmap]] U9): `compile_commands.json` showing the
CORRECT flags for a file is not proof the `.o` was actually rebuilt with
them.** After changing a per-file `-march` override in CMake, a rebuild's
`compile_commands.json` correctly showed the new flag, yet the crash the
fix should have resolved persisted byte-identically. An earlier `find
build-dir -name "*.o" -delete` followed by a targeted rebuild had silently
NOT reproduced that specific object file (absent from the "Building..."
build log entirely) -- only locating the exact `.o` path under
`CMakeFiles/<target>.dir/` and `rm -f`-ing it directly forced real
recompilation on the next build. If a rebuild's *behavior* doesn't match
what its *compile command* implies, don't trust the compile command --
delete the exact object file and rebuild again before doubting the fix
itself.

All done. `llama-completion` runs under `andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --runtime linux` — **6528953 cycles**, reproducible across two independent runs, and the full regression suite (14 driver tests + 44 andes_sim/vplat + 7 vlinux scripts + 55 e2e tests) is green with zero failures.

What it took, on top of what was already done before this session's final stretch:

1. **Four ELEN=32/vector-width bugs in llama.cpp's `ggml`**, all the same "QEMU permissive / real hardware enforces" pattern already seen 3x earlier in this roadmap, now at the vector-unit level:
   - `ggml_vec_dot_f16`/`_bf16`: GCC auto-vectorized a scalar fallback loop into illegal 64-bit vector ops. Fixed with a function-level `__attribute__((target("arch=rv64gc")))`.
   - `ggml_vec_cvar_f32`/`ggml_vec_soft_max_f32`: used an unnecessary 64-bit widening reduce that no other CPU architecture's code path needs. Rewrote to match its own siblings (32-bit reduce + scalar widen).

   - A stale ccache artifact that made one fix look like it hadn't applied when it actually just hadn't recompiled — a real gotcha, now in memory.

content.text:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

input.prompt:
You are reviewing a code diff for ALTITUDE issues only: is each change implemented at the right depth, or is it a fragile bandaid / special case layered on shared infrastructure instead of a deeper fix to the underlying mechanism? Do not look for correctness bugs.

Context: this diff is from a session that got a real llama-completion binary running under an "andesim" hybrid RISC-V simulator (QEMU + a cycle-accurate RTL simulator called vsim). Several ggml functions were crashing with illegal-instruction traps because they emitted vector instructions this hardware can't execute.

Two repos are involved:
1. `/home/nick/work/andesim` (the simulator driver, C++) — diff at `/tmp/claude-1002/-home-nick-work-andesim/5eeca9dc-9078-4a2c-9aec-f331d1142619/scratchpad/simplify_andesim.diff`

Read both diff files. Note: each diff is the FULL uncommitted diff of the touched files (nothing has been committed this session), so it may include some pre-existing uncommitted work from earlier in the same effort mixed in with the new work — focus your attention on what looks like genuinely NEW logic (added functions, added CLI flags, added helpers), not on isolated pre-existing lines that happen to be nearby.

Four fixes were applied to llama.cpp's ggml, each a DIFFERENT mechanism for what looks like a similar underlying problem (this hardware's vector-unit limits vs. what the code assumes):
1. `ggml_vec_dot_f16`/`ggml_vec_dot_bf16` in `vec.cpp`: fixed with a per-FUNCTION `__attribute__((target("arch=rv64gc")))` (a compiler-flag-level annotation on two specific functions).
2. `ggml_vec_cvar_f32`/`ggml_vec_soft_max_f32` in `vec.cpp`: fixed by rewriting the algorithm itself (removing an unnecessary 64-bit-element widening reduce, replacing with a narrower reduce + scalar widen).
3. `quantize_row_q8_0`/`quantize_row_q8_1` in `arch/riscv/quants.c`: fixed by deleting the vectorized implementation entirely and calling the portable scalar reference implementation instead.
4. (Already existed, elsewhere in the same CMakeLists.txt, not part of this diff but relevant context) a FILE-LEVEL `set_source_files_properties` march override for other generic dispatch files.

Read `/home/nick/work/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-cpu/CMakeLists.txt` around line 715-770 for the full picture of how these four mechanisms coexist (function-attribute, algorithm-rewrite, delete-and-fallback, file-level march). Judge: is having FOUR different mechanisms for variants of the same root problem (this target's vector-capability mismatch) a sign of accumulating special cases that should be unified into one deeper mechanism — e.g. a single documented policy or a build-time capability macro that each site checks — or is each one genuinely the right tool for ITS specific shape of problem (auto-vectorized scalar code vs. deliberate-but-wrong-precision intrinsics vs. no-narrower-alternative-exists)? The diff's own comments (read them) argue each is deliberately different because the underlying causes differ. Decide if you buy that reasoning or if there's a deeper unifying fix being missed.

Also check: `driver/cmd_run.cpp`'s new `--step-timeout-ms` handling — is bolting a manual parse-and-validate block directly into `cmd_run.cpp`'s run_hybrid() function the right altitude, or should this level of CLI-value validation live in `cli.cpp`'s parser itself (where `--mem-size` conceptually lives, even though its actual numeric parsing also happens at point-of-use in cmd_run.cpp — check that precedent)?

Report only real findings with file, line, a one-line summary, and what the deeper fix would look like. If you conclude the existing design is already at the right altitude, say so plainly and explain why in 2-3 sentences — do not manufacture a finding to have something to report. Keep the report under 400 words.

These three are genuinely different tools for genuinely different problem shapes, not accumulating cruft.

Mechanism 3 (`ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c:32-54`, `quantize_row_q8_0`/`quantize_row_q8_1`) is the real outlier. It doesn't gate the fix to the narrow-LMUL target — it deletes the `#if defined(__riscv_v)` capability check entirely, so the scalar fallback now runs unconditionally on *every* riscv64+GGML_RVV build, including a hypothetical/future full-spec LMUL=8 chip that has no problem here. Confirmed by checking `CMakeLists.txt:438-513`: this file compiles once per configured variant with no per-function capability dispatch, so there's no other mechanism recovering vectorization for capable hardware. The file's own surrounding convention (sibling functions at `quants.c:158,213,264,318,387,418,499` all still guard with `#if defined(__riscv_v)`) shows this pair is the one place that pattern was abandoned rather than followed. The comment even concedes a narrower fix was available ("QK8_0 is already an exact fit at LMUL=2... isn't worth re-deriving") — that's mechanism 2's approach, not applied here. Deeper fix: either rewrite at LMUL=2 like mechanism 2 did, or gate the scalar-only fallback behind the same capability signal mechanism 4 already established, instead of an ungated global deletion.

458	### 5.8 `--kanata <file>` (+ `--objdump <file>`) -- pipeline trace of the ROI
459	
460	Hybrid only (`--trigger marker|pc`). Writes a Kanata-format pipeline trace
461	covering exactly the measured window -- engine boot and handoff overhead
462	are filtered out. Open the file in
463	[Konata](https://github.com/shioyadan/Konata) to see the pipeline.
464	
465	```sh
466	./andesim run tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul.elf \
467	  --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium \
468	  --kanata /tmp/roi.kanata
469	```
470	
471	Add `--objdump <file>` (a text dump you generated once with
472	`riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump -d my.elf > my.S`) and the trace embeds the
473	disassembly next to each PC. `--objdump` requires `--kanata`.
474	
475	Marker-mode constraint: the ELF must contain exactly one exit marker. With
476	more than one, the run errors out and tells you to use `--trigger pc` with
477	an explicit `--pc-end` instead.
478	
479	### 5.9 `--gdb` (+ `--gdb-port <port>`) -- attach a debugger
480	
481	Pauses the simulation at startup so a debugger can attach. Not available
482	in hybrid mode.
483	
484	**fast** -- opens QEMU's GDB stub (default port 1234) and waits:
485	
486	```sh
487	./andesim run --mode fast --gdb my.elf
488	# other terminal:
489	gdb-multiarch -ex 'target remote :1234' my.elf
490	```
491	
492	**cycle** -- resets and HALTS the hart, opens the engine's JTAG bitbang
493	port (default 9104) in the background, then execs `$ICEMAN` -- your JTAG
494	debug server -- in the foreground. Point GDB at the server's own gdb port
495	(from your server config), not at 9104:
496	
497	```sh
498	export ICEMAN=/path/to/jtag-debug-server
499	./andesim run --mode cycle --gdb --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium my.elf
500	```
501	
502	`$ICEMAN` must speak the OpenOCD `remote_bitbang` protocol. A modern
503	**OpenOCD (0.12+)** works: a one-line wrapper can `exec openocd -f <cfg>`
504	where `<cfg>` sets `adapter driver remote_bitbang`, `remote_bitbang port
505	9104`, a generic `riscv` target, and a `gdb_port`. Note: the OpenOCD 0.10
506	bundled with Andes ICEman has a `remote_bitbang` bug against this DTM --
507	use a current OpenOCD.
508	
509	`--gdb-port` overrides the port (fast: the QEMU stub port; cycle: the
510	JTAG bitbang port).
511	
512	### 5.10 `--log-level <0-6>` (+ `--log-file`) -- how much andesim says
513	
514	The same scale as the vsim engines' own `--log-level`, so you learn one
515	scheme: `0=trace 1=debug 2=info 3=warn 4=error 5=critical 6=off`.
516	Default is `2` (info): you see your program's output, the answer line
517	(`[andesim] N cycles`), and any warnings or errors -- nothing else.

555	  Step qemu_step{kQemuId64, "fast-leg", trig};
556	  Step vsim_step{acc->id, "accurate-leg", trig};
557	  // --runtime linux + marker mode: vsim's OWN trigger only static-pre-scans
558	  // whatever ELF it is handed (hybrid::CsrTrigger::scan_buffer, vsim_andesim
559	  // src/hybrid/csr_trigger.hpp) -- but under --runtime linux vsim boots
560	  // vlinux-run.elf, and the marker HINTs are in the APP's ELF, which vlinux
561	  // only loads into memory at RUNTIME (never part of vlinux-run.elf's own
562	  // static PT_LOAD content). QEMU1's plugin has no such limitation (a TCG
563	  // plugin watches the EXECUTED instruction stream, content-agnostic), which
564	  // is why only vsim's leg needs a workaround here. Fix: resolve the exit
565	  // marker's PC by scanning elf_path (the app's real ELF) on the driver
566	  // side, using the SAME shared predicate vsim's own scanner uses
567	  // (hybrid/insn_match.h -- bit-for-bit the same match, not a reimplementation
568	  // that could drift), and feed it to vsim through the EXISTING PC-mode
569	  // trigger machinery (`--hybrid-exit-pc`, already wired for --trigger pc)
570	  // instead of marker mode. QEMU1 keeps ordinary marker-mode unchanged (its
571	  // detection already works); only vsim's own trigger config changes. This
572	  // needs ZERO changes to vsim's own source, matching the roadmap's explicit
573	  // "hybrid transport, triggers, plugin, resume driver, and engines need NO
574	  // changes" constraint.
575	  if (cli.runtime == "linux" && trig.kind == "marker") {
576	    const RoiMarkerPcs m = find_roi_markers(elf_path);
577	    if (m.exit_pc == 0)
578	      return fail("no ROI exit marker (slti x0,x0,0x5A1) found in " + elf_path +
579	                  " -- add <andesim/ROI.h>'s andesim_ROI_begin()/end() around "
580	                  "the region to measure");
581	    char pcbuf[32];

# Measuring one llama.cpp kernel iteration under andesim hybrid mode

This is the companion doc USER_GUIDE.md section 11 points to: the exact
patch that puts ROI markers around a matmul (or a short run of
consecutive matmuls) inside llama.cpp, how the target was chosen, and
the upstream `ggml` fixes a real build needs before it survives the
cycle-accurate leg's ELEN=32 vector unit.

Confirmed end to end:
- 2026-07-16: single iteration (K=51, layer 7's V projection) --
  **6528953 cycles**, stable across two independent hybrid runs.
- 2026-07-16: two consecutive iterations (K=51..52, V then K

## 6. Measuring N consecutive iterations

For a few consecutive matmuls instead of just one, set `ANDESIM_ROI_MUL_MAT_N`
alongside `ANDESIM_ROI_MUL_MAT_K` (both are build-time `-D`s -- no source
change). The marker begins at node K and ends at node K+N-1, so N=1
(the default when unset) is exactly the original single-iteration
behavior:

```sh
cmake -B build-rv64-static ... \
  -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="... -DANDESIM_ROI_MUL_MAT_K=51 -DANDESIM_ROI_MUL_MAT_N=2 ..." \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS="... -DANDESIM_ROI_MUL_MAT_K=51 -DANDESIM_ROI_MUL_MAT_N=2 ..."
cmake --build build-rv64-static -j --target llama-completion
```

Confirmed K=51..52 (V then K projection, both small): **13040043
cycles**, ~2x the single-iteration figure as expected.

**Keep N small.** The cycle-accurate leg runs at ~9 kHz; N=1 on the V
projection alone already needs ~13 minutes of wall clock (hence
`--step-timeout-ms 900000`+). Including one of the large matmuls (Q, O,
or any FFN projection -- see section 3's size ranking) in the range
multiplies the cost accordingly; a whole token (253 matmuls) is not
practical this way. Pick a short, deliberately small run of the
smallest-available matmuls, exactly like section 3 already argues for
a single iteration.

## 7. Dumping pipeline information (`--kanata`)

`andesim run --mode hybrid --kanata <file>` (see USER_GUIDE.md section
5.8) writes a Kanata-format pipeline trace of the ROI, viewable in
[Konata](https://github.com/shioyadan/Konata):

```sh
./andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --runtime linux --mem-size 2000M \
  --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --step-timeout-ms 900000 \
  --kanata /tmp/roi.kanata \
  /path/to/llama.cpp/build-rv64-static/bin/llama-completion \
  -- -m /path/to/models/Bonsai-4B-Q1_0.gguf -no-cnv \
     --prompt "The capital of France is" -n 32 -c 512 -t 1
```

No source or build change needed beyond what section 5 already has --
`--kanata` reads the same ROI markers the cycle measurement uses.
Confirmed on the K=51 single-iteration build: a 651 MB, well-formed
Kanata trace (`Kanata 0004` header, ~43.8M lines, event counts
consistent with 6528953 cycles). The trace is large in proportion to
the cycle count -- expect a correspondingly bigger file for a
multi-iteration (N>1) ROI.

**A real bug this surfaced, fixed as part of this work**: the driver's
`vsim_extra_args()` (`driver/hybrid.cpp`) unconditionally appended a
`--kanata-roi` flag alongside `--kanata` -- a flag that does not exist
anywhere in vsim (confirmed against vsim's own `--help` and its full
source tree), so every hybrid `--kanata` run failed immediately with
`Unrecognized option: --kanata-roi` before this fix. Root cause: vsim's
hybrid leg only ever executes the ROI in the first place (it resumes
at the trigger boundary and exits on the matching trigger), so plain
`--kanata` already produces exactly the "measured window only" trace
USER_GUIDE.md section 5.8 describes -- no separate "roi" flag was ever
needed on vsim's side. This had no automated-test coverage (the only
place `--kanata-roi` appeared besides the driver's own code was a
manually-gated block in `tests/e2e.sh` behind an unset-by-default
`KANATA_FILE` env var), so the bug was latent until `--kanata` was
actually exercised against a real vsim binary for the first time here.

content.text:
All tests green (14 driver + 44 sweep + vlinux hybrid ROI unaffected). Summary of this extension:

**N consecutive iterations**: `ANDESIM_ROI_MUL_MAT_N` (new build-time `-D`, default 1 = original single-iteration behavior) extends the marker to bracket nodes `[K, K+N-1]`. Verified with N=2 (V-projection + K-projection, layer 7): **13,040,043 cycles** — almost exactly 2x the single-iteration figure, as expected for two similarly-sized matmuls back to back.

**Pipeline dump (`--kanata`)**: found and fixed a real, previously-undetected bug — the driver sent vsim a `--kanata-roi` flag that doesn't exist anywhere in vsim (confirmed against its actual `--help` and full source), so every hybrid `--kanata` run failed immediately with "Unrecognized option." Zero automated test coverage had ever exercised this path against a real vsim binary. Fixed in `driver/hybrid.cpp` (plain `--kanata` already covers exactly the ROI window, since vsim's hybrid leg never executes anything outside it), corrected the test assertions in `hybrid_test.cpp` that had been asserting the broken behavior, and verified: a 651MB, well-formed Kanata trace against the real K=51 llama-completion build.

Kept N small per your note — I chose 2 (the two smallest available matmuls in this architecture) rather than anything larger, since even N=1 already needs ~13 minutes of wall clock on the cycle-accurate leg; the FFN and Q/O-projection matmuls are ~2.4x–4x more expensive each.

Docs updated (`docs/llama_roi_howto.md` sections 6-7, `ROADMAP_LINUX_RUNTIME.md` U9 addendum, memory file). Nothing new committed yet — let me know if you'd like this batch committed too.
